4: Asker wants to know why red-green color vision deficiency persists despite selection. Relevant passages explain the genetics or population prevalence of red-green color blindness, or document situations where dichromats perform as well as or better than trichromats (any task). Passages that only describe how normal color vision or cone cells work, with no bearing on persistence or advantage, are weakly relevant at most.
5: Asker wants to know whether twins can have different fathers. Relevant passages describe the reproductive mechanism by which one pregnancy can involve eggs fertilized by sperm from separate acts of intercourse, or document such cases. General passages about twins or about paternity testing without that mechanism are weak.
14: Asker wants to know what the colored shapes and 'darkness' seen with closed eyes are. Relevant passages name and explain the visual phenomenon seen without external light (its physiological source in the retina or visual system). Passages about eyelids, sleep, or dreams in general are weak unless they address this percept.
27: Asker wants to know why an electric current on the tongue produces a taste. Relevant passages describe taste elicited by electrical stimulation, or the ionic/transduction mechanism by which taste receptors respond. General passages about batteries or about the five basic tastes without the electrical link are weak.
29: Asker wants to know why a room looks reddish after time spent in blue-green light. Relevant passages explain the visual system's adaptation to the prevailing illuminant color and the resulting shift in perceived color afterwards (the cone-level or perceptual mechanism). Passages about cone anatomy alone or about unrelated optical illusions are weak.
37: Asker wants to know what prevents water from entering the body through the anus or genital openings while swimming. Relevant passages describe the anatomical structures that keep these openings closed at rest. Passages about swimming physiology, breath holding, or water pressure in general are weak.
39: Asker wants the mechanism by which non-ionizing UV causes cancer, and whether lower-energy light can do it. Relevant passages explain how UV photons directly damage DNA (the specific lesion types) or cause indirect damage, and how this relates to wavelength. Passages about sunburn, sunscreen, or ionizing radiation without the DNA-damage mechanism are weak.
49: Asker wants to know how biological brains learn, compared with backpropagation in artificial networks. Relevant passages describe biological learning rules at the synapse level (how connection strengths change with activity). Passages about artificial neural network math alone, or brain anatomy without learning mechanism, are weak.
54: Asker wants to know whether blood can be classified as an organ. Relevant passages give the definition or classification of blood as a tissue type, or the definition of an organ, so the two can be compared. Passages about blood composition or circulation with no classification angle are weak.
60: Asker wants to know why an iris without much melanin looks blue rather than another color. Relevant passages explain the physical optics of how blue eye color arises (how light interacts with the iris stroma) and the role of melanin. Passages about eye-color genetics or newborn development without the optical explanation are only partly relevant.
65: Asker wants to know why flash photos show red eyes in humans but green eyes in dogs. Relevant passages explain the red-eye effect (the source of the red reflection) and the reflective layer behind the retina in many animals that produces eyeshine. Passages about camera hardware alone or eye anatomy unrelated to reflection are weak.
68: Asker wants to know why acute hunger fades after a night's sleep. Relevant passages describe how hunger is regulated hormonally or by the circadian system, and how those signals vary across the day or with sleep. Passages about fasting, diet advice, or sleep in general without appetite regulation are weak.
75: Asker wants to know why the ring finger cannot move independently of the little finger. Relevant passages describe the hand's muscle and tendon anatomy (shared muscles or tendon interconnections) or the neural control of individual fingers. Passages about hand anatomy that do not bear on finger independence are weak.
79: Asker wants to know whether shortening light-dark cycles makes plants grow faster. Relevant passages describe plant circadian rhythms and what happens when the light-dark cycle period differs from the internal clock, or how photoperiod affects growth. Passages about grow lights or plant nutrition in general are weak.
84: Asker wants to know why funnel-web venom is lethal to primates but not to most other mammals. Relevant passages describe the venom's toxin and its molecular target, and any species differences in that target or in susceptibility. Passages about spider biology or first aid without the molecular or species-specific angle are weak.
98: Asker wants to know whether a tooth cavity can heal or refill. Relevant passages describe the tooth's tissue layers and which of them can regenerate or repair (and by what process), or whether early decay can reverse. Passages about dental hygiene or fillings without the biology of repair are weak.
